Cardiology and hematology · published research

Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Related mouse studies report less aneurysm enlargement or fewer wall disruptions after light exposure. A rabbit abstract reports changes in arterial mechanics, but PBM treatment evidence in people with abdominal aortic aneurysm has not been identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Three related mouse experiments report favorable changes in aneurysm growth or aortic-wall structure. A separate rabbit experiment reports differences in biomechanical measures, but the abstract leaves key methods unclear. No human treatment evidence is available for this condition.

Summary of the Evidence

Three mouse experiments from one research group report less aneurysm enlargement or fewer and smaller wall disruptions after PBM. A rabbit abstract reports changes in vascular mechanical measures, but provides limited methodological detail. These findings are preclinical and do not establish benefit in people.

Human and clinical evidence

No PBM treatment study in people with an abdominal aortic aneurysm was identified. A 2022 editorial discusses how light might be delivered to the deep aorta, but reports no patient treatment or clinical outcomes (Gavish et al. 2022).

Animal evidence

The 2009 mouse experiment studied aneurysm formation and progression after angiotensin-II infusion. At four weeks, enlargement of at least 50% occurred in 7 of 15 untreated mice and none of 13 laser-treated mice. The treated group also had less normalized aortic enlargement and better-preserved wall motion (Gavish et al. 2009).

A 2012 histology study of 32 mice found fewer and smaller wall disruptions and fewer macrophages at injury sites in laser-treated aortas. It also reported differences in smooth-muscle-cell size and collagen content in repair tissue (Gavish et al. 2012).

The 2014 study treated already-induced aneurysms. Further growth after early enlargement was seen in 7 of 12 controls versus 1 of 14 treated mice, with fewer severe aneurysms in the treated group (Gavish et al. 2014).

A 2021 rabbit e-poster abstract reports a calcium-chloride injury model and statistically significant differences in elastic modulus, resistive and pulsatility indices, radial and longitudinal strain, compliance, and distensibility (Mehrad and Ahmadi Noubari 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The three mouse experiments used a similar low-level laser setting: 780 nm near-infrared light for nine minutes. Reported fluence was 2 J/cm² in 2009 and 2012 and 2.2 J/cm² in 2014; the 2009 report also gave an irradiance of 4 mW/cm² (Gavish et al. 2009; Gavish et al. 2012; Gavish et al. 2014). These settings came from one related model line, not a dose-comparison study.

The 2009 and 2014 reports describe surgical access to the mouse aorta before irradiation. Such setups do not establish that light delivered through intact human abdominal tissues can reach the aortic wall at a comparable dose. The editorial discusses 780–870 nm light and proposes 2–4 J/cm² as a possible translational range, including delivery beside the aorta during laparoscopy; these parameters have not been clinically tested (Gavish et al. 2022).

The rabbit abstract describes 632 nm red light at 500 mW, applied with ultrasound guidance and parallel polarization. It does not report sample size, fluence, irradiance, or enough group and treatment detail to assess reproducibility (Mehrad and Ahmadi Noubari 2021).

Interpretation

The mouse experiments report less aneurysm enlargement and fewer or smaller wall disruptions in related models. The rabbit abstract adds biomechanical findings, but its methods are incompletely reported. Independent replication and evidence that PBM can safely deliver light to the human aortic wall would be needed before clinical benefit could be assessed.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for effects on aneurysm progression or wall stability in people. No human treatment study was identified; animal results cannot establish clinical benefit.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The three mouse experiments come from one research program and use closely related models, so they do not provide independent confirmation. The rabbit abstract adds a different animal model, but omits sample size and key treatment-dose details. No patient outcomes have been studied. Independent, fully reported replication and evidence of safe light delivery through intact human tissues are needed (Gavish et al. 2009; Gavish et al. 2012; Gavish et al. 2014; Mehrad and Ahmadi Noubari 2021).
